thread_analysis.thread_summary: Sharp USB PD / Bluetooth module product thread (1629 lines, long nested quote chain reaching back to 2023). Three key technical findings: (1) USB PD products require the AC adapter to be sent with the test sample; a relay board with GND and VBUS measurement leads (~10cm) must be prepared between the adapter and product for voltage monitoring — a fixed DC supply cannot substitute because USB PD negotiation requires the actual charger; (2) for products using a certified module but with a different antenna pattern, only 2 RF test items are required (Rx Sensitivity + Tx Output Power) — not the full 26 items, because this is an antenna design verification, not a full RF qualification; (3) for a Linux-based product implementing BlueZ as the Host Subsystem, referencing an unrelated third party's certified BlueZ QDID is technically possible but carries a takedown risk if the Listing Owner objects — the recommended path is purchasing a registration-ready stack from an established vendor, since raw open-source BlueZ has a historically ~60% first-pass rate on protocol/profile testing.
all_questions_found: How do we prepare voltage monitoring leads for a USB PD product for RF testing?
How many RF test items are required when only the antenna design is different from the certified module?
Can we reference an unrelated third party's already-certified BlueZ Host Subsystem QDID in our own registration instead of testing our own stack?
What test scope, pass rate, and lab logistics apply if we implement raw open-source BlueZ ourselves?
Does the Host Subsystem OS choice (Linux vs Android) matter for the 2-item RF test?
thread_analysis.key_technical_discussion: Three independent rules surfaced across this long thread: (1) USB PD requires physical protocol negotiation — only the real AC adapter can supply the correct voltage sequence, so a relay board is needed for voltage monitoring. (2) RF test scope is determined by what changed from the prior certification: if only the antenna changed from a certified module, only 2 antenna verification items (Rx + Tx) are needed, and the Host Subsystem OS (Linux vs Android) is irrelevant to this RF-only test since only the HCI layer and below are exercised. (3) Reusing another company's certified Host Subsystem QDID without a licensing relationship is registrable on paper but risks later cancellation if the Listing Owner notices and objects; raw open-source BlueZ implementation requires protocol/profile-layer testing with an ADB debugger and bilingual on-site lab presence, with a historical ~60% first-pass rate. Note: a much older (May 2023) buried question in the nested quote chain, asking whether End Product registration is required when Bluetooth is shipped disabled on a Windows PC and whether an OS-embedded Host Subsystem QDID can be reused, appears unanswered within this thread (no consultant reply located).
thread_analysis.key_decision_logic: USB PD → must send AC adapter + relay board. Modified antenna (only) → 2-item RF test scope, OS-agnostic. Host Subsystem QDID sourcing → must come from a properly licensed vendor relationship, not an unrelated third party's registration; raw open-source implementation shifts the risk to protocol/profile test pass rates.
thread_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: Sending a fixed DC supply for a USB PD product causes invalid test setup and test delays. Applying full 26-item scope for antenna-only change over-charges the customer. Citing an unrelated company's QDID risks SIG-initiated registration cancellation; raw open-source BlueZ risks high rework rates and project abandonment.
thread_analysis.consulting_mistake: No mistakes identified. All three rules were correctly applied during scoping and consulting.
thread_analysis.consulting_takeaway: Add USB PD to the pre-project sample preparation checklist: confirm power supply type, and if USB PD, request relay board with measurement leads. Always ask 'what hardware changed vs. the certified module?' to determine RF test scope (2 items for antenna-only change, 26 items for full RF qualification). For Host Subsystem stack sourcing, always verify the QDID being referenced is properly licensed to the customer — never an unrelated third party's registration — and set realistic pass-rate expectations if implementing raw open-source stacks.
